• Scientific name: Bagrichthys hypselopterus (Bleeker, 1852)
  • Common name: Black Lancer Catfish
  • Type locality: Palembang, Sumatra, Indonesia.
  • Synonym: Bagrus hypselopterus
  • Size: 400 mm or 15.7" SL.
  • IUCN Red List: Least Concern (last assessed 2018).

Members of the highly specialized and unusually-shaped bagrid catfish genus Bagrichthys Bleeker, 1858, live in large muddy rivers throughout Southeast Asia and are characterised by their elongate and laterally compressed caudal peduncle, the dorsally-directed serrations on the posterior edge of the dorsal-fin spine, gill membranes united but free from the isthmus, and a long adipose fin without a free posterior margin (Roberts, 1989).

It is very unlikely this fish has ever been available to the aquarium hobby.
Asia: Thailand to Indonesia. Pacific, Greater Sunda Island Rivers, Borneo Waters; Pacific, Greater Sunda Island Rivers, Sumatra Waters.

Asia: Sumatra and Borneo. Type locality: Palembang, in fluviis.

This species is reported from the Batang Hari and Musi River drainages in Sumatra, as well as the Kapuas River drainage in western Borneo.
Inhabits main rivers over muddy substrate, in deep waters with swift current.
In the wild, the fish are detritivorous.

The male 'black lancers' can be very territorial and as such can only be kept one male to a tank with the rest females. Although they possess a small mouth it is wide, but they don't tend to be a threat to other fishes as such, although if you keep very small fish with them they could be picked off at night as the lancer enjoys its night-time forays.
Males have an elongate genital papilla and longer barbels.

Etymology: The genus name Bagrichthys comes from 'bagre', a South American name for a catfish, but is only used for African and Asian species. The specific name hypselopterus means deep or long finned.

IUCN Red List: Extent of Occurrence (EOO) is estimated to be 247000 km2. Total population size and trend are unknown. Potential threats include deforestation resulting from logging, land conversion for agricultural use, and harvest for subsistence fisheries, but the impacts are unknown. Limited survey data suggests the species is uncommon throughout its range, but populations appear to be stable. It is assessed as Least Concern (IUCN 2019).
